query: For Q235 steel in its pre-exposure state, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain the onset or suppression of corrosion-related degradation in harsh environments at room and elevated temperatures? Specify a controlled study that would isolate the governing cause, predicted observations relative to the untreated reference, applicable boundary conditions, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive falsification result.

generation.hypothesis: The onset or suppression of corrosion-related degradation in Q235 steel at room and elevated temperatures can be explained by the formation of a protective coating, such as a high-entropy alloy (HEA) coating, which provides a barrier against corrosive environments.
generation.material_initial_state: Q235 steel in its pre-exposure state
generation.intervention: Application of a high-entropy alloy (HEA) coating, such as CoCrFeNiTix or CrMnFeCoNi, on the Q235 steel substrate
generation.conditions: Exposure to harsh environments, including 3.5 wt.% NaCl solution, at room and elevated temperatures
generation.structural_mediator: The microstructure and composition of the HEA coating, including the formation of a stable oxide layer
generation.mechanism: The HEA coating provides a barrier against corrosive environments, reducing the diffusion of corrosive species and preventing the formation of corrosive products
generation.predicted_outcome: Improved corrosion resistance of Q235 steel, with reduced mass loss and corrosion rate, compared to the untreated reference
generation.baseline: Q235 steel without any coating or treatment
generation.boundary: The temperature range of room temperature to 1000 °C, and the corrosive environment of 3.5 wt.% NaCl solution
generation.uncertainty: The optimal composition and microstructure of the HEA coating, as well as the effects of manufacturing defects and surface preparation on the corrosion performance

falsification_experiment.design: Controlled corrosion test, with Q235 steel samples coated with different HEA compositions and exposed to 3.5 wt.% NaCl solution at room and elevated temperatures
measurements: Microstructure and composition of the HEA coating
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the corrosion resistance of the Q235 steel samples with HEA coatings is not significantly improved compared to the untreated reference, the hypothesis is falsified

Since the δ of CMSX-2 was reported around −0.33%, its higher degree of misfit value would contribute to the higher strength. From a designer point of view, the tensile yield strength of HESA appears to be very stable from room temperature to 800 °C, which could be more favorable than conventional superalloys for gas turbine engine application. Regarding to creep behaviors, rafting can strongly affect the deformation at elevated temperatures. The coarsening of γ′ in CMSX-2 has been reported to be perpendicular to the stress axis (N-raft), so the N-rafted γ′ can provide interfaces with the formation of equilibrium interfacial dislocation network to hinder dislocation movements. By contrast, the creep of HESA is dominated by parallel raft (P-raft) and without perpendicular γ/γ′ interfaces. Tetzlaff et al. have reported that tertiary creep may dominate the creep response of P-rafted superalloys, and this is exactly the creep behavior observed for HESA at 982 °C. Therefore, higher creep rate of HESA compared to that of CMSX-2 could be a result of P-raft. According to a recent work on the thermal cycling creep of Ni-based superalloys, the P-raft of γ′ is proposed to be instead beneficial

In this work, (CoCrFeNi)95Nb5 HEA were selected as the composition of coating because of its high strength and corrosion resistance in bulk state, while the corresponding properties of coating remain unknown. Therefore, (CoCrFeNi)95Nb5 HEA coating on the Q235 steel substrate was fabricated by using the plasma spray technique, and the microstructure evolution during preparation process, microhardness, and corrosion behavior in 3.5 wt.% NaCl solution were investigated. Furthermore, the phase formation and the corrosion behavior of the coatings were specifically analyzed.

The corrosion resistance of Cr18Mn27Fe27.5Ni27.5 high entropy alloy in molten salts was tested after exposure to molten FLiBe salt at 700 °C for 1000 hours. The alloy lost significant mass compared to reference 316 H stainless steel which was attributed to the dissolution of Mn into the salt. The concentration of other elements in the HEA showed no significant change - most significantly the retention of much of the Cr in the alloy rather than dissolution into the salt is an important finding of this research. Elemental distribution and bulk x-ray diffraction showed that the alloy experienced the precipitation of a Cr-rich second phase. CALPHAD calculations confirmed this result via the prediction of a new BCC phase with approximately 4% phase fraction and a nominal composition of Cr67Fe13Mn18.5Ni1.5.

The effect of Ti content on the microstructure and corrosion resistance in a 3.5 wt.% NaCl solution was studied. The (Hf, Mo, Nb, Ta, Ti)B2 material was chosen for detailed high-pressure, high-temperature investigation because it is known to have the best thermal oxidation resistance of all the known transition metal borides up to 1200 °C [], and our preliminary mechanical property measurements indicate that (Hf, Mo, Nb, Ta, Zr)B2 has a high hardness value amongst HEB materials. In this study, we present a novel experimental approach where HEB material is synthesized under high pressures and high temperatures and its crystal structure and compressibility are studied under extreme environments in the same sample chamber without exposing the sample to ambient conditions, thereby minimizing contamination and generating data on high-purity HEB materials.
